1:
The psalm stands twice in Scripture, and every close reader works from that fact. Keil and Delitzsch call it the longest of all the hymnic psalms and think the original inscription was only the short one, the rest resembling the language with which songs of this class are introduced in the historical narratives. Adam Clarke notes that except for the first clause the title is taken from that narrative, and reports Kennicott’s view that the whole is a song of the Messiah, composed by David when his wars were at an end and divisible into five parts. John Calvin reads it biographically: David came to the kingdom through almost insurmountable obstacles, a fugitive till Saul’s death, then harassed by insurrections of his own subjects and by foreign enemies into old age, and having obtained his victories he does not, as irreligious men do, sing a song of triumph in his own honour. Augustine of Hippo reads the two names: David is by interpretation strong of hand and Saul is demanding, so that the psalm is Christ’s and the deliverance is from the king the people demanded against the will of God. Matthew Henry draws a lesson from the psalm having been handed to the precentor, that private compositions designed for a good man’s own use may serve the public, so that others borrow not only light from his candle but heat from his fire.

The opening line is itself a difference between the two texts. John Gill and C.H. Spurgeon both note that it is wanting in the historical version, Spurgeon calling it a most precious addition; Charles Ellicott would render it dearly do I love thee, and says the word strength strikes the keynote of the whole poem, which is a warrior’s song with a warrior’s conception of God. John Wesley notes that the Hebrew word means to love most affectionately and with the whole soul. On the string of titles that follows Adam Clarke takes them one at a time and numbers them, glossing the first as the craggy precipices that shelter men and wild animals and where bees make their nests, the second as a place fortified by nature and art, and the third as the God who causes him to escape — escapes so narrow that he plainly saw the hand of the Lord in them. Charles Ellicott distinguishes the figures more finely: the first word is better cliff and the second rock, giving the joint picture of a lofty precipice with a castle on its crest; and the horn of salvation alludes not to an animal’s weapon but to a mountain peak, since peaks are called horns in many languages, so that the phrase should be rendered my peak of safety.

The fourth verse divides on a single noun. Charles Ellicott says the Hebrew may mean either birth pangs, as the Greek and a New Testament citation take it, or cords; the hunter’s snares in the next verse fix it as cords there, so the same rendering is best here — though he adds that the version in Samuel, waves of death and billows of ruin, is probably the true reading, since the parallelism requires it. Adam Clarke keeps the cables and makes them the stratagems in which he was almost taken, while the floods are troops of wicked men rushing like an irresistible torrent, one wave impelling another. John Wesley reads them as dangerous and deadly troubles breaking in like a flood. John Gill refers the sorrows to the snares laid for David and, beyond him, to the whole grief of Christ’s life and chiefly to the garden. On the cords of the grave Adam Clarke asks whether the reference is to the ropes by which a corpse is lowered or the bandages in which the dead were swathed, and John Gill takes it of the winding-clothes that bound the dead hand and foot.
7:
The theophany is the most admired passage in the psalm and the commentators say so. Adam Clarke quotes a description of it as truly sublime and noble and in the genuine spirit of poetry, with God surrounded by all the powers of nature as his attendants and arming heaven and earth to fight his battles. Charles Ellicott says the whole realm of poetry cannot show a finer feeling for nature in her wrath, and then tracks the storm through its stages: first the rumbling of the earth, probably an earthquake preceding the storm or only its distant threatening; then the thunder-cloud forming, with intermittent flashes playing about the distant summits; then the dark masses of rain-cloud bending to earth under the tread of God; then the momentary lull so common before the final fury bursts; then the lightning darting through the curtain of cloud; and at last the wind and its effects on the earth’s surface. John Wesley holds the whole to be figurative expressions denoting the greatness of God’s anger, and that the coming down is not by change of place but by the manifestation of his presence.

On the smoke from the nostrils Adam Clarke explains that the ancients placed the seat of anger in the nose, since violent passion shows itself in the heated breath, so that physiognomists reckoned wide nostrils a sign of a fiery disposition. John Gill reads the whole as a storm of thunder, the smoke being thick black clouds, the fire lightning and the coals thunderbolts, and takes the imagery to be borrowed from the giving of the law on the mount. The cherub of the tenth verse draws the entry’s most interesting agreement. Charles Ellicott says the passage alone would show how naturally the idea of winged attendants grew out of the phenomena of cloud and storm, since we need only think of the giant pinions into which cloud shapes itself, though much of the developed conception came from contact with Assyrian art; and he reports the conjecture that the word should be read as chariot rather than cherub. Keil and Delitzsch report the same conjecture, then argue against it from a supposed relationship between the biblical cherub and the Indo-Persian griffin, on which the word would signify a creature that seizes and holds irrecoverably fast. John Wesley and John Gill both take the cherubim for the angels, whom God uses in raising such storms.

Both commentators reach for poets to carry the description. Adam Clarke sets beside the cherub the lines on the chariot of paternal Deity rushing forth with whirlwind sound, flashing thick flames and conveyed by four cherubic shapes. Charles Ellicott is denser still, quoting within a few verses the earth groaning as if beneath a heavy load, a translated chorus in which a god glides on the back of a quick-winged bird, the silence in the heavens before a storm when the bold winds are speechless and the orb below as hush as death, a modern poet on fire and sky becoming one brief ecstasy and then ashes, and the passage in which both ends of heaven pour fierce rain with lightning mixed, water with fire, in ruin reconciled. On the channels laid bare Adam Clarke refers the verse to an earthquake, since the rending of the ground makes water gush out at the fissures, and instances an earthquake in Jamaica in which whole rivers were poured out of the chasms and new lakes covered a thousand acres of land. Charles Ellicott takes the channels for torrent beds, or, with the version in Samuel, the depths of ocean, and John Gill hears an allusion to the drying up of the sea at the exodus.
16:
Charles Ellicott calls the sixteenth verse an exquisite transition from the real to the figurative: the parted waters of the storm become the floods of affliction named earlier, so that God rescues the sufferer by means of the very tempest sent in answer to his prayer to overwhelm his enemies. He would render it more forcibly, that God laid hold of him and drew him out of great waters, and holds that the conception behind it is of the gates of death lying under those floods, which being parted the sufferer can at last be reached. Adam Clarke keeps the allusion running: the waters were sweeping the people away and God interfered to draw David out, though he allows that waters sometimes denote multitudes of men, which the following verse seems to countenance. John Gill supplies the missing object of the sending, canvassing the hand, help from the sanctuary, the word of command, and, with two Jewish commentators, the angels — and applies the whole to the resurrection, when an angel rolled away the stone as a token of discharge.

Who the strong enemy is divides the entry. Adam Clarke proposes a particular occasion, the conflict with the giant’s son who thought to have slain David and from whom Abishai rescued him, after which David’s men swore that he should go no more out with them to battle lest the light of Israel be quenched; he adds that David had been nearly exhausted by the fatigue of the day when the giant took his advantage. John Gill offers a ladder of candidates: as it respects David, the Philistine champion or Saul; as it respects his antitype, the chief priests and Pharisees, or Satan the strong man armed with all his powers, or death, the last enemy, from whose cords he was loosed at the resurrection.

On the enemies preventing him Charles Ellicott would render it that they fell upon him unawares, noting that the verb is generally used in a good sense; John Wesley says simply that they had almost surprised him, and Adam Clarke that they took advantage of the time when he was least able to make head against them. John Gill refers the day of calamity to the garden and the cross, a day dark and cloudy in both a literal and a spiritual sense. On the large place Charles Ellicott hears a direct historical allusion to the settlement of Israel in Canaan, as a comparison of the Hebrew with the promises of the exodus will show. Adam Clarke makes it military, that David was enabled to clear the country of foes who had before cooped him up in holes and corners. John Wesley takes it as a state of freedom and comfort after straits, and notes that the psalmist ascribes all his mercies to God’s good pleasure as their first spring. John Gill makes it heaven itself, spacious enough for Christ and all his people. Charles Ellicott notes in passing that these three verses show only trifling variations between the two copies of the psalm.
20:
The claim of righteousness in these verses is felt as a difficulty and each voice handles it differently. C.H. Spurgeon states the problem plainly: read as prophetical of the Messiah the words are easy, but as David’s own language they have perplexed many. His solution is to distinguish two orders. In the dealings of providence there is often a discernible rule of justice by which the injured are at length avenged; David’s troubles arose from charges brought against his character under cover of Saul’s malice, and those charges he declares utterly false, asserting a grace-given righteousness which God rewarded in defiance of his calumniators. Before God the man after God’s own heart was a humble sinner; before his slanderers he could speak without blushing of the cleanness of his hands. There is no self-righteousness, he adds, in an honest man knowing that he is honest, nor in believing that God rewards him in providence for it; but it would be self-righteousness indeed to carry such thoughts out of providential government into the spiritual kingdom, where grace reigns not only supreme but sole.

John Gill answers by exclusion: if the words are applied to David they cannot mean his own personal righteousness or any works of righteousness done by him, since these merit nothing at God’s hand, are imperfect, are unprofitable to him, are no more than his duty even at their best, and are in fact filthy rags. Matthew Henry keeps the claim but limits its court: the deliverances cleared his innocency before men and acquitted him of the crimes he was falsely accused of, so that being rewarded according to his righteousness means the determining of a controversy; and he observes that when the troubles continued long David may himself have begun to suspect himself. Adam Clarke and John Wesley both narrow the righteousness to a single relation, that David was Saul’s friend and not his enemy and dealt righteously with a man who dealt unrighteously with him, keeping his hands pure from his blood.

On keeping the ways of the Lord John Gill distinguishes the ways God himself walks in from the ways he prescribes, takes the second, and grants that David kept them with delight and constancy but not perfectly, having many a slip. Adam Clarke makes it a matter of religious observance, that he was neither an infidel nor a profligate but trusted God and carefully observed the ordinances of his religion. On the judgments set before him John Gill takes the precepts of the law as a rule of walk and conversation, abolished as a covenant of works but kept in view impartially, and adds that this was fulfilled in the highest sense by Christ. John Wesley says only that he diligently studied and considered them. The last clause, about keeping himself from his own iniquity, produces the entry’s one confession of ignorance. Adam Clarke takes it for what is generally termed the easily-besetting sin, the sin of a man’s constitution or that to which the temperament of his body most powerfully disposes him — and then declares that what this was in David is a subject of useless conjecture. John Wesley agrees that it is the sin he was most inclined or tempted to, and Adam Clarke adds that the times of David’s greatest affliction were the times of his greatest uprightness, adversity being to him always a season of spiritual prosperity.
25:
The principle that God meets men as they meet others is stated by all and grounded differently. Adam Clarke calls it the general tenor of God’s providential conduct towards mankind and sets beside it a poet’s prayer that the mercy shown to others may be the mercy shown to us, and the petition in which we ask forgiveness as we forgive. John Wesley puts it as measure for measure. John Gill inverts the order of causation with care: it is not that men are first merciful and God then merciful to them, for he has mercy on whom he will have mercy, and their mercifulness is neither the cause nor the condition of his; rather, to those who have already received grace he shows fresh mercy and bestows more.

The hardest clause is the one that makes God froward, and the two closest readers work it from the same root. Adam Clarke takes the noun for the perverse man, crooked in his tempers and ways, and the verb as setting oneself to twist, twine and wrestle: if he contend, God will contend with him, follow him through all his windings, untwist him in all his cunning wiles and defeat his schemes of stubbornness and fraud. He quotes his old Psalter, which renders it that with the wicked thou shalt be wick, and observes that the word wicked is there used in its true original sense of crooked or perverse. Charles Ellicott notes that one English word stands for two Hebrew ones, both from roots meaning primarily to twist, so that the metaphor may describe either a character twisted awry or a line of conduct bent and crooked; our own word, being from-ward as against toward, leans to the second. The sense, he says, is that God will turn away from those who turn away from him — a thought he calls true even under the Christian revelation, and illustrates from the line that he who shuts love out shall in turn be shut out from love. John Wesley says it in seven words, that God will cross him and walk contrary to him.

On the lamp Charles Ellicott would render it that God makes his lamp bright, notes that the version in Samuel says instead that the Lord is his lamp, and observes that light is an emblem of prosperity or of life itself and is used very frequently of David and his family. Keil and Delitzsch say the same from the word’s form: the lamp is life burning on and on, with prosperity and high rank included, and in a related form it is the usual figurative word for the continuance of David’s house. Adam Clarke hears a promise that the family shall not become extinct, and suggests the Messiah may be the lamp meant. John Gill canvasses outward prosperity, inward spiritual light and the estate of Christ’s kingdom. The running through a troop is read three ways: John Gill reports renderings that make it running to meet a troop with intrepidity, running after one in pursuit, and breaking one in pieces, and prefers the last; Charles Ellicott would put the verbs in the present and read that by God he scatters a troop and scales walls, calling it a graphic reminiscence of warlike exploits; and Adam Clarke looks for a particular siege, suggesting the taking of the stronghold from the Jebusites. Matthew Henry observes that David owns the hand of God in every step of his advancement, including the military skill he was neither bred to nor designed for, his genius leading him rather to music and poetry; and C.H. Spurgeon makes the two clauses cover both kinds of siege, the open field and the battlements, since whether hemmed in by living legions or by stone walls the outcome is the same.
30:
Adam Clarke takes the perfect way to mean that God’s conduct is like his nature, absolutely pure, and notes that the word given as tried means literally tried in the fire. Charles Ellicott presses the same figure to sterling gold rather than dross, and observes that a verse in the Proverbs seems to be taken from this one. John Wesley applies the perfection to providence, which may sometimes be dark but is always wise and unblameable, and the trying to the promises. John Gill allows that the methods of providence are cavilled at by wicked men and murmured at by God’s own people, who are at a loss to reconcile promises with providences, but holds that when the judgments are made manifest the wisdom of them will be admired. On the question who is God besides the Lord Charles Ellicott notes that rock was a common term for their divinities among the tribes of Canaan, while Adam Clarke reads it as a fountain emitting continual supplies of grace.

The soldier’s equipment occupies the middle verses. Adam Clarke explains the girdle as a necessary part of eastern dress, which supported the loins, confined the garments and carried the sword, and says the strength of God was to David’s soul what the girdle was to the body. Charles Ellicott adds that the girdle is essential to the warrior and to all active exertion, and that the way here is not conduct but the military march; Keil and Delitzsch gloss the shield of salvation as the shield that consists of that salvation. On the hinds’ feet both close readers reach for the same poet: Adam Clarke notes that speed of foot was a necessary qualification of an ancient hero and that the swift-footed epithet is Homer’s standing honour for his own, and Charles Ellicott cites the same invariable epithet. John Gill allows the swiftness to be for flight or for pursuit and applies it to running the ways of God’s commandments. On the bow both correct our version: Adam Clarke says a bow of steel is out of the question, since in David’s day the making of steel is not likely to have been known, and all the versions render it brazen; Charles Ellicott would read that his arms bend a bow of copper, and for the test of strength compares the famous bow of Ulysses, which the great master drew with ease.

The verse about hands taught to war produces the sharpest disagreement in the psalm. John Gill draws the plain inference, that from this it appears war in some cases is lawful, and that all the skill of training men, marshalling armies and forming sieges is from God. Adam Clarke, on the same words, first observes how few of the conquerors of mankind could say their success was owed to divine help, and then breaks out: war is as contrary to the spirit of Christianity as murder; nothing can justify Christian nations in shedding one another’s blood; all men should and might live in peace, and the nation that is first to break it lies under a heavy curse. On the gentleness that made him great Charles Ellicott defends the plain rendering against the versions, which have discipline instead: we cannot afford to sacrifice this striking foreshadowing of the saying about being meek and lowly to the scare of a word like anthropomorphism, and there is no more reason to fear calling God meek than calling him jealous. Adam Clarke keeps the meekness but turns it inward, that God enabled him to bear and forbear, behaving with courage in adversity and humility in prosperity; and he gives his old Psalter’s version of the other reading, that the chastising suffers him not to err from the end to come.
37:
John Gill looks for occasions and finds them, referring the pursuit and overtaking to the recovery of what the Amalekites had carried away, on the authority of a Jewish commentator, and allowing that the wounding was true of all David’s wars. On the necks of his enemies Adam Clarke takes the gesture literally: treading on the neck was the triumph of the conqueror and the utmost disgrace of the vanquished, so the phrase means that David was made a complete conqueror. Charles Ellicott gives the Hebrew as saying that God gave him the back of his enemies, which either means that they were turned to flight so that only their backs were visible or alludes to that same symbolism of trampling. John Gill prefers the first, that they were made to turn their backs in an utter rout.

Whose cry goes unanswered is the entry’s question. Adam Clarke divides the verse between two sets of enemies: the Philistines called upon their gods and there was none to save, while the clause about crying to the Lord covers such men as Saul and Absalom, who professed to worship the true God and called on him while opposing David — and God no more heard them than the idols heard the Philistines. John Gill reads the first clause as looking round to see whether any were near to help, notes that the version in the history has looked where this has cried, and reports the view that they cried to their idols, as the mariners in the story each cried to his own god. Keil and Delitzsch take both clauses of the same people: the prayer was wrung from them by distress and was offered both to their gods and to the Lord, and it failed because it was made for their own cause and put up too late.

The last verse of the section is a problem of grammar as much as of imagery. Keil and Delitzsch observe that one does not pulverize dust but to dust, so the comparison must describe the result rather than the material: they became as dust before the wind. Charles Ellicott collates the two texts and finds the differences instructive, the history having the weaker phrase of the earth for before the wind, and stamp and tread them out where this has cast them out, while the Greek gives grind or pound; he takes the sense to be sweeping them before him. John Gill makes the phrase a figure of utter and irrecoverable ruin, comparing the image of the four monarchies broken to pieces and made like the chaff of the summer threshingfloor. Adam Clarke supplies the history instead, and says the words well express the manner in which David treated the Moabites, the Ammonites and the people of Rabbah, who were put under saws and harrows and axes of iron.
43:
Whether the strivings are domestic or foreign is the entry’s first question. Charles Ellicott says the parallelism favours taking the word as peoples, that is the Gentiles, but that since the version in the history has my people the phrase should be explained of David’s early political troubles. Adam Clarke takes it so without hesitation, of disaffections and insurrections among his own subjects, the revolt of Absalom and the civil war on behalf of Ishbosheth; and he identifies the people he did not know as the Syrians, Philistines and Edomites, all brought under tribute. John Wesley divides the verse the same way, and John Gill adds the tribes who after Saul’s death refused to acknowledge David until they anointed him at Hebron. On the strangers submitting Adam Clarke reports a rendering that has them lying to him rather than submitting, and offers two senses — that his own sworn subjects broke their obligation and followed his rebellious son, or that the subdued nations promised cordial obedience while their hearts felt enmity. Charles Ellicott gives the same clause as coming with flattery, and would render the fading away as withering before a scorching blast and the coming out of close places as coming trembling out of their castles.

The close is a doxology and is handled as one. C.H. Spurgeon presses the first clause: we serve no inanimate, imaginary or dying God, and like loyal subjects we should cry, long live the King of kings. Adam Clarke makes him the source whence help may at all times be derived. John Gill unfolds the living: God has life in himself, essentially and independently, and is the author of life to all creatures, natural life to all men and eternal life to his chosen. On the avenging John Gill is careful to separate private revenge, which belongs to no one, from the public vengeance a magistrate may exercise, and thinks the phrase rather designs the victories God gave. Adam Clarke reads it as God keeping down the spirits of the disaffected, and Keil and Delitzsch hear in the whole close the blessing of the knowledge of God reaching the heathen.

The verse about giving thanks among the heathen is quoted by the apostle, and both commentators say so. Adam Clarke adds an observation from an early writer that the prophecy is fulfilled to this day, since there is no town, village, hamlet, country or even desert where Christians dwell in which God is not praised by their singing the psalms of David. Charles Ellicott uses the same verse against the psalm’s traditional date: it seems almost too magnificent a thought in David that he could draw the surrounding nations within the circle of the religion as he had drawn them within the dominion of Israel, and it is not likely that an individual would speak so, which is why the verse is adduced by those who assign a later date — though he allows that the nations may be only an unwilling audience of the conqueror’s praises. On the last verse he reports that many treat it as a late liturgical addition, the change to the third person being suggestive though not conclusive, and then states his conclusion about the whole problem: each of the two copies has been again and again claimed as the original, and the best explanation of the variations is that both are independent copies of some original, this one having been altered in preparation for choir use. Adam Clarke ends on the word for ever, which he takes to run through all the duration of created worlds and then beyond, into the eternity that is beyond time.
